Photometry Formulas and Error Calculations

This document provides detailed mathematical documentation for the photometric calculations used in the pipeline.

Table of Contents

  1. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (S/N)

  2. Magnitude Error Calculation

  3. Error Propagation

  4. Quality Flags

  5. References

Signal-to-Noise Ratio (S/N)

Formula

S/N = flux / flux_error

Where:

  • flux: Source flux (background-corrected and aperture-corrected, see below)

  • flux_error: Uncertainty in flux measurement (σ_flux), including the uncertainty of the local background estimate

Implementation Details

Aperture Photometry:

  • Computes the background-corrected flux aperture_sum_bkg_corr from a robust sigma-clipped median annulus and uses it for the magnitude, its error and the S/N (a single, consistent flux)

  • flux_error is aperture_sum_bkg_corr_err, i.e. the quadrature sum of the aperture error, the local-background error and the centroid term. This column is produced by detection_and_photometry and drives the magnitude error, but it is not retained in the exported catalog

  • No rounding applied to preserve precision

PSF Photometry:

  • Uses flux_fit from PSF model fitting

  • flux_err from PSFPhotometry is already the standard deviation (not variance)

  • A local background is subtracted per source before fitting. A sigma-clipped median annulus (LocalBackground, radii 2× and 3× FWHM) is evaluated per source and the values are passed as the local_bkg column of the PSF-fitting init_params. This matches the aperture-photometry local background and removes residual sky/nebulosity that would otherwise bias the fitted flux and its error. Sources whose annulus is fully masked or off-frame fall back to no local subtraction rather than returning a NaN fit.

  • The empirical PSF itself is built from de-contaminated cutouts: the same local-background annulus is subtracted from a copy of the image around each PSF star before extract_stars, so the ePSF is not built from sky-contaminated stars. On a synthetic frame with a constant sky pedestal this drops the PSF flux bias from ×2.5 (no local background) to ×1.001.

  • Shape and dimensions. The PSF is fitted in a compact fit_shape (≈3× FWHM, rounded to an odd number of pixels) but the ePSF is extracted from a larger ≈5× FWHM cutout, so the wings are not truncated and normalised away; this keeps the encircled-energy correction (which reaches 1.5× FWHM) meaningful. The ePSF centre is (N − 1) / 2 on its oversampled grid.

  • Star selection. Candidate ePSF stars are filtered on flux, S/N, shape, crowding and a local-background flatness test. Truly saturated pixels are already removed by the pipeline mask, so the saturation check is only a last-resort guard and never rejects the brightest unsaturated stars; an approximate S/N derived from sqrt(flux) is not used as a hard cut.

PSF-vs-aperture consistency check. After photometry, check_psf_aperture_consistency() matches PSF and aperture sources by position and reports the median psf_mag − aperture_mag for each aperture. Both methods are placed on the same total-flux scale (see the aperture correction above), so the difference should be centred on zero. A median offset larger than PSF_APERTURE_CONSISTENCY_THRESHOLD (0.15 mag) raises a warning; the per-aperture counts, medians and robust (MAD) scatter are stored in st.session_state["psf_aperture_consistency"]. The per-source value is also exported for every aperture as psf_minus_aperture_mag_X_X (with filter-prefixed aliases), NaN where only one method measured the source; the zero point is common to both magnitudes and cancels in the difference. The results view plots the per-source offset against the calibrated PSF magnitude (with per-aperture median and zero lines) and as a histogram. Note that photutils subtracts local backgrounds per source over its own fit_shape cutout; for the crowded case this does not bias the recovered flux in practice (verified on grouped pairs with symmetric and strongly asymmetric pedestals), so the local background is kept for overlapping sources rather than zeroed.

Aperture Correction

The S/N is invariant under a multiplicative flux correction, but the instrumental magnitude is not. Before computing magnitudes the aperture flux is corrected for the fraction of the PSF that falls outside the aperture using the encircled-energy curve of the empirical PSF (or an analytic Gaussian fallback):

flux_total = flux_aperture / EE(r)

The correction factor 1/EE(r) is stored per source in the apcorr_X_X column, and the encircled-energy fraction it came from in ee_fraction_X_X (so a large correction is traceable to a poorly-enclosed aperture rather than a silent magnitude offset). This puts aperture and PSF photometry on the same total-flux scale, which matters because the zero point is anchored to one aperture.

The zero point is fitted against the aperture-corrected instrumental_mag_X_X column. The instrumental_mag_bkg_corr_X_X column is the uncorrected, background-subtracted reference (useful for diagnostics) and does not anchor the calibration.

Aperture-correction systematic. The correction shifts the (log) flux by a relative amount (apcorr - 1)/apcorr. Unlike the statistical flux error, this shift does not cancel in the flux ratio, so it must be added to the magnitude error separately:

sigma_apcorr = MAG_ERR_COEFFICIENT * f_apcorr * |apcorr - 1| / apcorr

where f_apcorr is the fractional uncertainty of the correction (APCORR_SYSTEMATIC_FRACTION in src.pipeline, default 0.20, i.e. the correction is trusted to 20% of its size). The per-aperture term is stored in apcorr_mag_err_X_X and combined in quadrature with the statistical magnitude error. It dominates the error budget at high S/N, where sigma_mag alone is very small. Setting APCORR_SYSTEMATIC_FRACTION = 0 disables it.

Example

# For a source with 1000 counts and error of 10 counts:
flux = 1000.0
flux_error = 10.0
snr = flux / flux_error  # = 100.0

Magnitude Error Calculation

Formula

σ_mag = 1.0857 × (σ_flux / flux)

Where:

  • σ_mag: Magnitude error (instrumental)

  • σ_flux: Flux uncertainty

  • flux: Source flux

  • 1.0857 = 2.5 / ln(10)

Mathematical Derivation

Given the magnitude-flux relation:

mag = -2.5 × log₁₀(flux)

Using error propagation:

σ_mag = |∂mag/∂flux| × σ_flux
      = |-2.5 / (flux × ln(10))| × σ_flux
      = (2.5 / ln(10)) × (σ_flux / flux)
      ≈ 1.0857 × (σ_flux / flux)

The statistical term above is combined in quadrature with the aperture-correction systematic sigma_apcorr (see the Aperture Correction section), which does not cancel in the flux ratio:

σ_mag = √( (1.0857 × σ_flux / flux)² + σ_apcorr² )

Relationship to S/N

For high signal-to-noise sources (S/N > 5), the statistical term reduces to:

σ_mag(stat) ≈ 1.0857 / S/N

This is valid because:

σ_mag(stat) = 1.0857 × (σ_flux / flux)
            = 1.0857 × (1 / (flux / σ_flux))
            = 1.0857 / S/N

At high S/N the actual exported σ_mag is dominated by the σ_apcorr systematic and the zero-point term rather than by 1.0857 / S/N.

Example

# For a source with flux=1000 ± 10:
flux = 1000.0
flux_err = 10.0
mag_err = 1.0857 * flux_err / flux  # = 0.01087 mag

# Verify with S/N:
snr = flux / flux_err  # = 100.0
mag_err_from_snr = 1.0857 / snr  # = 0.01087 mag (same!)

Error Propagation

Sky Background Model

Two independent background estimates are used, and they play different roles:

  • a global 2D model (Background2D, SExtractor mode estimator) defines the per-pixel background and background_rms arrays. The RMS map is the “background-only” noise term of the per-pixel error map (σ_bkg below);

  • the local annulus median removes whatever sky level the global model left behind around each source (see the next section).

The per-box RMS uses the MAD-based estimator (MADStdBackgroundRMS). The plain standard deviation of the sigma-clipped box is biased high by the wings of undetected sources: measured on synthetic frames it over-estimated the true pixel noise by x1.11 at 15 px source spacing, x1.38 at 12 px and x2.03 at 10 px, and that factor propagates straight into every flux error. The MAD estimator is unbiased on a clean frame (x1.02) and stays much closer when crowded (x1.17 at 12 px).

The smoothing filter over the background mesh is capped at 3x3 when the mesh is small (< 12 boxes across). A 5x5 median filter over an 8x8 mesh over-smooths the model: on a 300 ADU sky ramp the subtracted frame was x2.24 noisier than the raw frame, whereas a 3x3 filter leaves x1.54.

Finally, the model never aborts the run. Background2D discards any box with more than exclude_percentile % of masked/clipped pixels (10 % by default), which can reject every box in a crowded field or a frame with large bad areas and raise ValueError. The estimation is retried with 50 % and then 100 % tolerance and a coarser box, and if no mesh is possible it falls back to a single sigma-clipped background level for the whole frame. That last-resort _constant_background model uses the same MAD-based RMS as the normal path, so fallback frames do not get a source-inflated noise map. Aperture photometry stays usable in that case because each source still has its local annulus background subtracted.

For consistency with the error model, the source-detection threshold is also derived from the MAD-based global scatter (stdfunc="mad_std") rather than the plain sigma-clipped standard deviation. The plain std is inflated by undetected sources, which would silently raise the effective detection threshold above the requested threshold_sigma in crowded fields.

Local Background Subtraction and its Error

The local background is measured as the sigma-clipped median of the annulus surrounding the source (ApertureStats), not a plain mean, so neighbouring sources and cosmic rays do not bias it. For an aperture area A_ap and an annulus area A_ann:

bkg_per_pixel     = sigma-clipped median of the annulus
total_bkg         = bkg_per_pixel × A_ap
sigma_bkg_pixel   = annulus_median_err        # sqrt(pi/2) × s / sqrt(A_ann)
sigma_total_bkg   = sigma_bkg_pixel × A_ap
flux              = aperture_sum − total_bkg
σ_flux²           = σ_aperture² + σ_total_bkg² + σ_centroid²

Because the local background is a median, its uncertainty is the standard error of the median, sqrt(pi/2) × s / sqrt(A_ann) (~1.2533× larger than the mean-based s / sqrt(A_ann)), which is what ApertureStats.median_err returns. Using the mean’s standard error for a median underestimates the local background term by ~25% and σ_flux by ~8% in the background-limited regime. When median_err is unavailable (older photutils, or non-finite values) the pipeline falls back to the mean-based estimate.

Centroid-Position Error

A fixed aperture samples a different fraction of the PSF when the source is not perfectly centred. The corresponding flux error is

sigma_pos   = sigma_PSF / S/N            # per-axis centroid uncertainty
sigma_pos   = clip(sigma_pos, 0.01, 0.5 × FWHM)
sigma_flux  = 0.5 × sqrt( (F(x+σ)-F(x-σ))² + (F(y+σ)-F(y-σ))² )
σ_flux²     = σ_aperture² + σ_total_bkg² + σ_centroid²

sigma_PSF = FWHM / 2.3548 and F(...) is the aperture sum re-measured with the aperture shifted by ±sigma_pos along x or y (centroid_flux_err_X_X). Using the measured shifted sums rather than a symmetric-Gaussian derivative is intentional: for a perfectly symmetric PSF the linear term vanishes by symmetry, whereas the real (asymmetric/elliptical) PSF does contribute. The term is small for apertures larger than the PSF (a few percent of the statistical error) but matters for small apertures and undersampled PSFs.

The σ_total_bkg term is essential: omitting it underestimates σ_flux by roughly 20% for the default r_in = 2r, r_out = 2.5r annulus and therefore overestimates the S/N by the same amount in the background-limited regime.

Calibrated Magnitude Error

When converting instrumental magnitudes to calibrated magnitudes using a zero point:

mag_calib = mag_inst + zero_point

The error propagates as:

σ_mag_calib = √(σ_mag_inst² + σ_zero_point² + σ_sys²)

This is quadrature addition because the errors are independent. The zero point is a median of the calibrator residuals, so its formal uncertainty is the standard error of the median,

σ_zero_point = √(π/2) × scatter / √N ≈ 1.2533 × scatter / √N

over the retained calibration stars (N), kept at full precision. The √(π/2) factor (about 25% larger than the mean-based scatter / √N) is exported as MEDIAN_STD_ERROR_FACTOR in src.pipeline.

The scatter in this expression is taken from the sigma-clipped sample before the |residual| <= 0.5 mag hard cut. That hard cut removes the tails and biases the truncated (“retained”) scatter low; since the sigma clip already removes true outliers, the wider sample is the best available estimate of the intrinsic dispersion. Both values are recorded on the matched calibration table (zero_point_scatter, zero_point_scatter_kept) and the diagnostics are stored in st.session_state["zero_point_diagnostics"].

An optional systematic floor σ_sys (default 0) is supplied through the systematic_floor argument of add_calibrated_magnitudes and is resolved per run by resolve_systematic_floor():

  1. analysis_parameters["systematic_mag_err_floor"] / session state,

  2. the RPP_SYSTEMATIC_MAG_ERR_FLOOR environment variable (headless runs),

  3. the module default SYSTEMATIC_MAG_ERR_FLOOR (0, i.e. no extra term).

The zero-point uncertainty is now propagated into every exported aperture_mag_err_* and psf_mag_err column by add_calibrated_magnitudes(zero_point_std=...).

Random vs correlated components. σ_zp (and σ_sys) is a common offset shared by every source in the field, not an independent per-source error. Adding it in quadrature is conservative for a single source, but it does not average down over an ensemble. To support both uses, the total error is accompanied by two explicit component columns for every magnitude-error column:

aperture_mag_err_1_3           = sqrt(random^2 + correlated^2)   (total)
aperture_mag_err_1_3_random     = per-source statistical error plus the
                                   aperture-correction systematic
_aperture_mag_err_1_3_correlated = sqrt(σ_zp^2 + σ_sys^2)          (field-common)

The same _random / _correlated suffixes exist for psf_mag_err, but the PSF random component is the PSF-fitting statistical error; it has no aperture-correction term. For relative photometry, quote _random; for absolute photometry, use the total. The field-level zero_point_std is also stored as a catalog column.

Example

import numpy as np

# Instrumental photometry with error
mag_inst_err = 0.05  # mag

# Zero point calibration with uncertainty
zero_point_err = 0.03  # mag

# Propagated error
mag_calib_err = np.sqrt(mag_inst_err**2 + zero_point_err**2)
# = √(0.05² + 0.03²) = √(0.0025 + 0.0009) = √0.0034 ≈ 0.058 mag

Effective gain

The per-pixel error map is built with calc_total_error(background_subtracted_data, background_rms, effective_gain). The effective gain (counts per data unit) is resolved in this order:

  1. FITS conversion keyword, in the priority order of GAIN_KEYWORDS: explicit EGAIN and CCDGAIN (already e-/ADU) and CVF (a conversion factor in ADU/e-, so gain = 1/CVF) are tried before the conventional GAIN. The value must be positive and inside the plausible range 0.02-100 e-/ADU (GAIN_PLAUSIBLE_RANGE); anything outside it is reported and ignored. On a recognised driver-gain camera a bare GAIN is skipped entirely (see below);

  2. user-supplied gain — the Detector Gain parameter in the sidebar, analysis_parameters["effective_gain"], or the RPP_EFFECTIVE_GAIN environment variable for headless runs (0 or empty means automatic);

  3. empirical photon-transfer estimate from the frame itself: for boxes of pure sky the pixel variance grows linearly with the mean signal,

    var(box) ≈ read_noise² + mean(box) / gain

    so 1 / slope of a robust fit to (mean, variance) is the effective gain. The estimate is accepted only when the frame really constrains it: enough source-free boxes (sigma clipping removes < 10% of the pixels), a sky level that varies enough across the frame (slope measured at ≥ 3σ), and a physically plausible result. A flat sky carries no gain information and is rejected;

  4. effective_gain = 1 (data treated as electrons) as the last resort, with an explicit warning.

Step 4 is the conservative choice, but it is not neutral: with data in ADU and an unknown true gain g, the source Poisson variance flux/gain is overestimated by a factor g, i.e. the magnitude errors of bright sources by up to √g. The previous arbitrary 65535 / max(image) heuristic remains removed.

The Poisson term must follow the units of the frame

calc_total_error adds data / gain to the pixel variance, which only carries information when the data are counts and the gain is expressed in those same units. A frame that has been rescaled — a normalised float stack with a sky level of about 1e-2, or the output of a stacking tool that divides by a large factor — breaks that assumption: with a genuine e-/ADU gain the Poisson term at the sky level then exceeds the measured sky variance by orders of magnitude, so the error map no longer describes the real noise (aperture S/N was underestimated by one to two orders of magnitude on such a frame).

The PSF step is the most sensitive consumer, because photutils weights the ePSF-to-star fits by 1 / error²: with the inflated core errors the star cores carried ~1e-4 of the weight of the sky pixels, most fitted fluxes came back negative, the next ePSF was built from inverted cutouts and EPSFBuilder aborted with Cannot normalize ePSF: the data sum (…) is not finite and positive, dropping PSF photometry for the whole frame.

The gain is therefore validated against the frame itself in resolve_poisson_gain():

  • the resolved gain is kept when the Poisson variance it predicts at the sky level stays within POISSON_SKY_VARIANCE_TOLERANCE (10×) of the measured background variance;

  • otherwise it is replaced by the largest value the frame allows,

    gain = sky_level / background_rms²

    because the sky Poisson variance cannot exceed the total sky variance, so the true gain in the data’s units is at least this large. Using that bound gives the largest (most conservative) Poisson term the frame admits, correct to within a factor of ~√2 at the sky itself;

  • frames with no usable gain or no usable sky statistics keep their declared gain, and compute_error_map() falls back to the background RMS map alone when no Poisson term can be trusted.

On a real normalised stack this changed the core error from ~1.4e3 × the sky RMS (larger than the data values themselves) to a few × the sky RMS, restoring both the aperture S/N and the PSF photometry.

Why a FITS GAIN is not always e-/ADU

CMOS cameras expose an adjustable analog gain whose driver setting is written to GAIN, but that number is not a conversion factor. QHY writes an abstract 0-100 scale (a QHY268M operated in high-gain mode at GAIN=56 measures ≈0.77 e-/ADU, and the HGC/LGC switch sits at 55→56); ZWO ASI writes a 0.1 dB value whose unity-gain setting is model-specific (e.g. ≈100 for the ASI2600). The mapping from the driver setting to e-/ADU is per-model and piecewise, so the pipeline does not try to guess it: it recognises such a camera from the instrument metadata (INSTRUME/INSTRID/INSTRUMENT/CAMERA/DETECTOR/ CCDNAME, matched by DRIVER_GAIN_INSTRUMENT_PATTERNS) and ignores its bare GAIN, then uses an explicit EGAIN/CVF conversion, the user-supplied gain, or the photon-transfer estimate measured from the frame itself. Supplying the true conversion factor for the gain setting in use (read from the manufacturer’s gain-vs-e-/ADU chart) is the most reliable option.

The same resolved gain is handed to astroscrappy.detect_cosmics for the cosmic-ray mask, together with a RDNOISE/READNOIS/ENOISE value when the header provides one. A cosmic-ray mask covering more than MAX_CR_MASK_FRACTION (20%) of a frame is not physical and is discarded rather than removing a large part of the science image.

Masked pixels (border, cosmic rays, satellite trails and NaNs) are excluded from both the source and the annulus photometry.

Atmospheric Extinction (Optional)

If atmospheric extinction is applied:

mag_calib = mag_inst + zero_point - k × airmass

Where:

  • k: Extinction coefficient (mag/airmass)

  • airmass: Air mass during observation

Error propagation becomes:

σ_mag_calib = √(σ_mag_inst² + σ_zero_point² + σ_sys² + (airmass × σ_k)²)

Color-Term Calibration (Optional)

When catalog colors are available for a matched source, the pipeline can also apply a simple linear color-term correction after the standard zero-point calibration.

Baseline calibrated magnitude:

mag_calib = mag_inst + zero_point

Color-corrected calibrated magnitude:

mag_calib_colorcorr = mag_calib + color_term_offset

The fitted offset is modeled as:

color_term_offset = intercept + C × (color - color_ref)

Where:

  • C: fitted color-term coefficient

  • color: per-source catalog color, for example BP-RP or g-r

  • color_ref: median color of the retained calibration stars

  • intercept: residual offset relative to the scalar zero point

This follows the same first-order idea described in STDPipe, while keeping the existing scalar zero-point calibration as the compatibility baseline.

Uncertainty of the color correction. The fit parameter covariance is taken from the final least-squares fit (scatter² × (Dᵀ D)⁻¹) and propagated to each source through its color offset x = color - color_ref:

var(color_term_offset) = var(intercept) + 2x·cov(intercept, C) + x²·var(C)

It is stored in color_term_offset_err (and color_term_std / intercept_std are returned by the fit). Every color-corrected magnitude gets a parallel error column *_colorcorr_err:

σ_mag_colorcorr = √(σ_mag_calib² + σ_color_term_offset²)

where σ_mag_calib is the baseline calibrated error (already including the statistical, aperture-correction and zero-point terms). Sources without a usable catalog color keep NaN in every correction column.

Practical Limitation

Color-corrected magnitudes are only written for sources that have the required catalog color columns in the final table. Unmatched sources, or sources without usable catalog colors, keep the standard zero-point-calibrated magnitudes only.

Quality Flags

Sources are assigned quality flags based on their S/N:

Quality Flag

S/N Range

Description

Recommendation

'good'

S/N > 10

Reliable photometry

Use for science

'marginal'

5 < S/N ≤ 10

Intermediate quality

Use with caution

'poor'

S/N ≤ 5

Unreliable photometry

Exclude from analysis

'unknown'

N/A

Missing/invalid data

Exclude

Rationale

  • S/N ≤ 5: Detection may still be real, but the photometry is too uncertain to be labeled reliable

  • 5 < S/N ≤ 10: Usable for inspection or exploratory analysis, but not in the highest-confidence class

  • S/N > 10: Conservative threshold for reliable photometry with smaller magnitude uncertainties

Usage Example

import pandas as pd

# Load photometry catalog
df = pd.read_csv('photometry.csv')

# Filter for reliable sources only
reliable_sources = df[df['quality_flag_1_1'] == 'good']

# Include marginal detections with warning
usable_sources = df[df['quality_flag_1_1'].isin(['good', 'marginal'])]

Implementation Notes

Numerical Precision

  • All S/N calculations use full floating-point precision (no rounding)

  • This prevents divide-by-zero errors in magnitude error calculations

  • Magnitude errors are computed directly from flux ratios, not from S/N

Edge Cases

The implementation handles several edge cases:

  1. Negative background-corrected flux: Kept as-is in the S/N (it is a real non-detection rather than silently replaced by the raw flux) and excluded from the magnitude/error columns (nan)

  2. Zero flux: Produces nan magnitude and nan magnitude error

  3. Very low/high flux: Maintains numerical stability across dynamic range

  4. Missing data: Assigns 'unknown' quality flag

  5. Masked / NaN pixels: Excluded from both the aperture and the annulus sums and from their errors via the shared pipeline mask

  6. Unreliable photometry: a source is removed only when every photometry method reports a magnitude error of 2 mag or more (MAG_ERR_MAX in src.tools_pipeline, overridable per run through the Max Magnitude Error parameter). A source with one usable method is kept, and sources without any error information at all (all NaN) are kept as well. Setting the parameter to 0 disables the cut completely, leaving the quality flags as the only reliability indicator.

Testing

Run the test suite to verify calculations:

pytest tests/test_photometry.py -v
